content: For hepatitis C virus (HCV) screening, in settings with a higher prevalence of infection (10%), strategies using either rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) or enzyme immunoassays (EIAs) demonstrated comparable performance and cost. However, using a single EIA test may not be efficient in these higher-prevalence settings. With an assumed 26% loss to follow-up, only strategies employing a single test for active infection achieve an NPV greater than 95%. Additionally, one-step strategies that directly test for active HCV infection identify a substantially higher proportion of infections. At a 40% prevalence, with 26% of individuals not returning for follow-up testing, the model shows that only strategies directly testing for active HCV infection achieve an NPV greater than 95%. Among diagnostic tests for active HCV infection, qualitative HCV RNA testing is preferred due to its higher sensitivity compared to quantitative RNA testing, which results in slightly more false negatives at a similar cost. Countries with existing investments in quantitative RNA platforms or those leveraging HIV testing infrastructure may still find quantitative RNA testing practical. If quantitative RNA is anticipated for monitoring HCV therapy, it may also be used for initial HCV testing. HCV core antigen (Ag) testing, at its current cost, is less accurate and more expensive than RNA-based tests. However, if the cost of core Ag testing decreases significantly, it could become an attractive option despite its slightly lower sensitivity and specificity. In high-prevalence settings (10% or higher), the most sensitive diagnostic test should be used to minimize false negatives, as nearly all positive tests represent true positives. Qualitative HCV RNA testing emerges as the preferred option due to its superior sensitivity. Strategies using quantitative RNA or core Ag testing often result in worse test performance and higher costs compared to qualitative RNA testing. HCV prevalence significantly influences the choice of testing strategy. In very high-prevalence settings, minimizing false negatives and avoiding missed cases become the primary considerations. When same-day testing is not feasible, a one-step strategy directly testing for active HCV infection is recommended. In summary, while no single HCV testing approach is universally efficient, multiple strategies can be employed depending on the prevalence and available resources. The choice between EIA and RDT should be guided by in-country cost and feasibility. If same-day testing is not possible, direct testing for active infection is the most effective approach.
